idea: "Who is allowed to be wrong?" The bank never, so it sizes on the 1-in-100 case. The sponsor may be wrong in the good case, so it hopes on the expected case. The cheques are the bank's; the gift is the sponsor's.
sources: S2 #4 (Renewables Valuation Institute page); FUSIONS C device

idea: Japan's "negative spread". Life insurers promised about 4% (5.5-6.5% pricing in 1995) on money still to be invested, while assets earned about 2% after 1990. The gap hit the whole book for a decade. Nissan Mutual failed on 25 April 1997, the first postwar life-insurer failure, and others followed.
sources: Nippon Life Research Institute report id=51079; Nogami, SOA International Section News, May 2016; Wikipedia "Nissan Life"; CEPII letter 196 (2000)
use: The coupon soft spot at full scale. Japan's gap was on 100% of the book every year; Laura's is on the reinvested coupons only, once (TNA note 1 names this risk). Laura's own size: a 2pt fall in yields costs about $21k of the $500k (IPS_number_sheet, 16 Oct; MODEL, old design). Device: a table of a 1989 insurer beside Laura, same promise length, same 2pt fall.
critique: It was not only rates: property, loan and share losses, and policy surrenders, all played a part. CEPII's "Ponzi-style" is a journalist's word. Counts differ (8 failures per Nogami; "six of the eighteen" per CEPII). Chiyoda failed probably in October 2000, not 1999. Window: Nogami says JGBs rose from 11% to 42% of life insurers' asset mix 1995-2015, which is not "the survivors then bought".
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened NLI, the SOA pdf, Wikipedia and CEPII); counts CONFLICTING
clash: Partly. S1 says the gap is "covered in about 93 of 100 paths by the order of cover in the plan". That old order leaned on the VT half, and the FINAL says no payment depends on a share price, so the FR must cover the gap from Treasuries.
where: S1 §1 l.19-68; FUSIONS §2 item 6; README l.71

idea: Equitable Life's guaranteed annuity rates (UK, 1957-2000). A free option (each £100 buys £10 a year) was sold with no price and no reserve. When rates fell from 1993, the board cut payouts to those who took it. The House of Lords ruled against it on 20 July 2000, adding about £1.5bn to liabilities; the society closed to new business on 8 Dec 2000 with assets of about £34bn.
sources: Geneva Association, "Equitable Life" case study (2016) pdf; Wikipedia "Equitable Life Assurance Society v Hyman"
use: "What we announce, we own": a named failure behind the FINAL's "whatever figure you choose is money you already own". It is also the structure Caplet avoids, a guarantee resting on a share-heavy base. Device: the chain 1957-88 free option, 1993 no reserve, 2000 court, December 2000 doors close.
critique: Three things are blended: a rate option, longer lives and discretionary bonuses. It was "a promise written without a price", not "a promise too big", and also a regulatory and disclosure failure. The ten payments do not fit (no option is written on them).
verified: VERIFIED through a second-hand summary of the Geneva Association pdf (S1); not quoted verbatim

idea: Dutch funding-ratio zones and conditional indexation. A fund's one number is assets over liabilities (x100%). Below about 104% the fund must take measures; between 104% and 110% there is no indexation; at 110% or more, indexation may be granted. The Dutch abandoned the regime: under the new system "the funding ratio no longer determines whether benefits rise or fall".
sources: De Nederlandsche Bank, "pensions funding ratio" page (paraphrase); Future of Pensions Act detail UNVERIFIED (Houthoff page not opened)
use: The cliff lesson: share a fixed fraction (half the shares) rather than all or nothing at a line. A three-zone "repair / hold / share" picture for co-sponsors.
critique: The thresholds are cliffs. The ratio moved with the discount rate, so cuts came when yields fell. Indexation means inflation-linking, which Laura's nominal payments lack. The procyclicality story comes from background reading and was not re-verified.
clash: Partly. A "repair" zone implies trading in response to a ratio, and the FINAL allows only two reasons to change. Use only the "half, not all" sharing lesson.

idea: Why the cushion is thin: about 1.00x cover is right for bought cash flows, and buffers exist for unmatched risk. Laura's ~102% sits under the Dutch 104% buffer, and her 1.006x sits under a project's 1.20-1.30x DSCR; FUSIONS gives headroom of $1,139 (3.8bp, A01).
sources: DNB page (S1 #3); Renewables Valuation Institute and Forvis Mazars DSCR pages (S2 #4); Model Suite A01
use: Answers a judge's "why so little slack?": the copied part needs no cushion, and the only cushion belongs to coupon reinvestment.
critique: Stale: 102% and 1.006x used the 16 Oct curve, and cover was 1.004x on 22 Oct (Conflict 7). CLAUDE.md (6 Nov, 5 Nov curve, MODEL) puts the ladder at $302,163, so cover is now below 1.00x, which is exactly the case the FINAL's COMPLETE2028 handles.
verified: Sources VERIFIED (S1, S2); cover figures MODEL (old design) and superseded
clash: No, it fits COMPLETE2028. Never quote 102% or 1.006x.

idea: Germany's maximum guaranteed rate (Höchstrechnungszins). The regulator caps what an insurer may guarantee at a cautious portfolio's expected yield less a 40% safety margin (at least 0.4pt in low-rate phases). The rate was 4.00% from July 1994 to June 2000, 3.25% from July 2000, 2.25% in 2007-11, 0.90% in 2017-21, 0.25% in 2022-24 and 1.00% in 2025; the DAV recommends 1.0% for 2027.
sources: DAV (German Actuarial Association), "Höchstrechnungszins in der Lebensversicherung" pdf; PwC Germany insurance-news blogs (articles 240720 and 252092)
use: Answers "why promise only half?". Regulators haircut what may be promised because sellers under competitive pressure cannot be trusted to cap themselves. The top of Laura's band is her own maximum guaranteed rate, and the FINAL's kept half is her haircut: the same instinct, not the same number.
critique: It protects new customers only, and it is blunt (one rate for all). It fell to 0.25%, making guarantees almost unsellable. The 40% is a judgement. The Swiss BVG comparison was not opened.
verified: VERIFIED (S1; paraphrase of the DAV and PwC pages)

idea: Germany's additional interest reserve (Zinszusatzreserve, since 2011): when an old guaranteed rate rises above the reference rate, the insurer must build the reserve now, not when the gap bites.
use: The regulator's version of "price the reinvestment gap and set it aside early" (the 24 Oct K-fix; Synergy B's 2031 re-measure). With Japan: every insurer that waited paid more.
critique: Costly; it was a repair for old 4% contracts.
clash: Partly, as Synergy B. It is a set-aside the FINAL does not state; fine if it comes from Treasuries or 2028 money as a pre-set rule.

idea: Ruin theory with risky investment. With the reserve in cash, the chance of ruin falls exponentially as capital grows; with the reserve in a risky asset it falls only as a power, and if 2a/sigma^2 < 1, ruin is certain.
sources: Frolova, Kabanov and Pergamenshchikov, "In the insurance business risky investments are dangerous", Finance and Stochastics 6 (2002) 227-235; arXiv 2012.05083 (intro); arXiv 1505.04331
use: "Cushion in bonds, shared upside in shares", and "you cannot buy certainty in the asset that is trying to beat you" (a short Portfolio Analysis box).
critique: The result is asymptotic and assumes an infinite horizon, random claims and premium income, none of which Laura has. Window 28 Oct: an analogy, not a theorem-backed reason. The 1-in-10 to 1-in-100 figures are illustrations only.
verified: VERIFIED (S1 opened the DOI abstract and the arXiv intros)

idea: The classical Cramér-Lundberg ruin model: seems relevant, isn't, because it needs random claims and Laura's are known to the dollar.
use: One FR "considered and rejected" line.

idea: Solvency II's two boxes. A cash flow that "can be replicated reliably" using instruments with an observable market value is valued at the copy's price, with no separate risk margin. Only what cannot be copied (policy options, mortality, expenses) carries a margin.
use: Ten fixed nominal $50k payments are the cleanest replicable cash flow there is, and Treasuries are the copy, so the price of the promise is the price of the ladder. Coupon reinvestment is the part not replicated "in amount and timing", and its reserve is Laura's "risk margin" (the $10k-$20k hold-back option, number sheet decision 3; MODEL, old design). Device: a two-column page, "bought" and "reserved".
critique: Art. 40 says nothing about coupon reinvestment. "Replicable" is a judgement. The risk margin's calibration is a policy number.
verified: VERIFIED (77(4) quoted from legislation.gov.uk; Art. 40 paraphrased)
clash: No: the bought box is the FINAL's LADDER and FLOOR. Any hold-back sizing is not in the FINAL.

idea: The zero-premium stress test. Solvency II Art. 18 does not count a future premium the payer cannot be compelled to pay, so count the 2028 deposit as zero and ask "would the payments hold if it never arrived?"
sources: Delegated Regulation 2015/35 Art. 18 (legislation.gov.uk); R06 and L-10 (22 Oct curve)
use: Honest answer for the FR: usually, not always. The ladder costs more than $300k in 46-47% of paths (median gap about $9.8k), filled from the 2028 deposit. A cheque breaks only if yields fall about 2pt and the deposit falls by more than about 56% (M3); with a coverage rule the cheques survive a deposit of about $40k (M5). All MODEL, old design. This ties CAREER to COMPLETE2028, since the 2028 deposit is career income.
critique: Window 28 Oct: S1's "Yes" is FALSE on Keel's own numbers. Art. 18 is an analogy, not an authority.
verified: Art. 18 VERIFIED; S1's answer CONFLICTING (corrected by the Window and FUSIONS Conflict 1)
clash: YES as S1 wrote it ("the ladder is bought from the 2027 money alone"): the FINAL says the 2028 deposit completes the ladder if yields fall. The corrected form fits.

idea: Deferred income annuities and mortality credits: seems relevant (a lump sum now, fixed income later), isn't. Without a mortality pool, an annuity is a ladder plus the insurer's margin, and annuities are not WInS-permitted.
sources: Kitces, "Understanding the role of mortality credits"; Milevsky on Yaari (1965), "my lunch with Professor Menahem Yaari"; the "Scott 2008" attribution was not found and was dropped
use: FR "alternatives considered": an insurer would sell Laura this ladder and charge for it, and the only thing that justifies the charge is a pool of people dying, which she does not have. Kitces's example: a ladder supports about $57.43 a year per $1,000 against about $98.86 from a pooled annuity (25 years, 3%).
critique: Insurer credit risk, fees, no way out. The "collapses to a ladder" step is the scout's inference, not a source's claim.

idea: Smith-Wilson extrapolation and the ultimate forward rate (EIOPA): seems relevant, isn't. It is a rule for extending the curve beyond the last liquid point, and Laura's last payment (2042) sits inside the liquid Treasury curve.
sources: EIOPA and PwC pages (found, not opened)
use: One FR "considered and rejected" line.

idea: GMWB annuities: the closest insurer analogue to a guaranteed payment funded by a risky portfolio, and a possible later answer to "why not a guarantee on shares?"
use: A possible FR line; Equitable (row 12) is already the stronger answer.

idea: Pension and insurance seeds not opened and dropped: the Swiss BVG minimum rate, the detail of the Dutch Future of Pensions Act, the UK Pension Protection Fund, CPF LIFE, Norway's spending rule, AP7 and tontines.
use: None

idea: Brady bonds (1989). Defaulted bank loans were rewritten into bonds whose principal was locked in specially issued 30-year US Treasury zeros held at the New York Fed, while the coupons stayed exposed (some had short rolling guarantees). Ecuador defaulted on its Bradys in 1999; Mexico retired its in 2003.
sources: Wikipedia "Brady Bonds"; Susmel, University of Houston course page (bauer.uh.edu/rsusmel/7386/brady.htm)
use: "The 1989 twin": lock what must not fail in dated Treasuries, let the rest float, and tell the buyer which is which. That is the FINAL's floor fund plus VT, done at national scale, and it justifies stating the bottom and the top at different confidence levels.
critique: The protection was partial and did not prevent later defaults. The vault was bought with borrowed multilateral money. Mathematically it is just a zero plus a risky bond; the novelty was packaging and transparent pricing. The "12-18 month" rolling guarantee is UNVERIFIED. Laura is the investor, not the debtor, and her risky half is shares she owns, with price risk but no default risk.
verified: VERIFIED (S2 via fetch-tool summaries; re-check quotes before citing)
clash: No, provided the FR says Brady's vault was Treasury zeros, which Laura cannot buy (STRIPS are banned). Her vault is coupon bonds and iBonds, which carry reinvestment risk.

idea: The Brady "stripped yield" as a method for the 2031 range. Price the protected principal as a Treasury zero, subtract it, and read the price of risk from what is left. For Laura: strip what is owned (the floor) and quote only the leftover with a probability. Mexican pars' stripped spread went from 254bp (31 Dec 1993) to 452bp (31 Mar 1994).
sources: Susmel, University of Houston course page
use: FR co-sponsor text: quote the bottom as owned and the top as a probability-weighted leftover. Three tools, one range: Brady strips, P99 covers, the newsvendor places.

idea: Pitt's sinking fund (1786): £1m a year plus its interest to buy back debt. It worked from 1786 to 1793 while there was a surplus; with war borrowing from 1793 it bought debt with borrowed money. Walpole's earlier fund was raided; Pitt's was abandoned in the 1820s. Robert Hamilton of Aberdeen (1813), not Alexander Hamilton, exposed the fallacy.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund"; Hansard, Commons, 11 Mar 1823 (a cost "equal to a perpetual annuity of 268,000l."; "voted away 324,000,000l."); econbiz full text of The Industrial Revolution (author unconfirmed: the fund "lulled the mind of the ministers"; £271m and £618m borrowed); Wikipedia "Robert Hamilton (economist)"
use: "A promise to save is not a vault": the FINAL buys the payments in January 2027 instead of scheduling savings for them. FR section "what we refused to do". Keel's analogy: paying down a mortgage from a credit card you have not paid off.
critique: The fund was mis-fed, not pointless (the 1823 defenders), so "sinking funds are fraud" is unfair. Price's "penny at the birth of Christ" and Pitt's 1792 rule are UNVERIFIED and dropped. S2 itself notes "the owned bottom is only owned once the 2028 deposit has arrived".
verified: VERIFIED in parts (S2, fetch summaries); part of the Wikipedia date chain is tagged [citation needed]
clash: Partly. S2 says the 2028 money funds "only the floor and the stocks, never the ten payments"; the FINAL says it completes the ladder if yields fall.
where: S2 §2 l.88-148; FUSIONS §2 item 5; README l.72

idea: Ricardo's test: "No sinking fund can be efficient for the purpose of diminishing the debt, if it be not derived from the excess" of revenue over spending. Ask of every dollar the plan counts on: does it exist, or is it promised?
sources: Ricardo, Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, ch. 17 (marxists.org)
use: The $300k exists in January 2027; the 2028 $150k is promised (career income). The honest answer under the FINAL: the ladder is bought with money that exists, and only a gap (if yields fall) waits on the deposit, as its first call.
critique: FUSIONS Conflict 1: the test "tests the 2027 gap". The ladder costs more than $300k in about 47% of paths (MODEL, old design), so the strong form fails.
verified: VERIFIED (quote from the marxists.org text, via S2)
clash: No in the honest form; yes if stated as "no payment waits on money not yet earned".

idea: Pitt's anti-raid rule. What Pitt got right was making the money hard to raid by law. A stated rule and a public range do the same for Laura against her own future self.
sources: Wikipedia "Sinking fund" (Pitt's 1786 law "stopped ministers from raiding the fund in crises")
use: Backs the FINAL's "only 2 possible reasons we would change our plan" as an anti-raid rule; links to rules over discretion and commitment devices (C R02 47-49).
critique: Pitt's law did not stop the wartime circularity: a rule protects the money only while its source is real.

idea: Perry v. United States (1935). In the one time the US rewrote a bond term (the 1933 gold-clause abrogation), the Court called the abrogation invalid as applied to the bond. But Perry recovered nothing, because he could not show a loss of buying power, so the rewrite stood: "a right with no remedy". The line "as much bound by their contracts as are individuals" is Chief Justice Waite's, from the Sinking-Fund Cases (1879), quoted in Perry.
sources: Cornell LII, 294 U.S. 330; Window 28 Oct correction; FUSIONS header correction (Felix, huddle H-003)
use: Answers "what if the government changes the rules?". The only term ever rewritten was a gold clause, and Laura's bonds are plain dollars. The risk the Court named, buying power, sits on the facility side, which is why the kept half exists. Device: "which clause broke in 1933, and does Laura's bond have one?"
critique: It is a gold-clause case, not about ordinary nominal Treasuries. The "political compromise" reading is UNVERIFIED. It says nothing about debt-ceiling delays (C R02 13). Never write that the Treasury "cannot rewrite a bond", or that terms were "broken": they were "rewritten" once.
verified: VERIFIED (Cornell LII); S2's "cannot rewrite" gloss CONFLICTING (corrected)
clash: No, if worded per the corrections. It supports "barring a US default".

idea: The late Treasury bill payments of April-May 1979: some bill redemptions were paid late. With 1933, these are the only blemishes on the US payment record that the files name.
sources: Felix's correction (huddle H-003); no outside source cited
use: The honest edge of "barring a US default": the near-miss was a delay. That is one more reason each holding matures before its January (C R02 13).
critique: None recorded. It concerns bills, which Laura does not hold directly.

idea: Project-finance two-test sizing. Lenders size debt on both P50 (the expected case, at about 1.20-1.30x DSCR) and P99 (the 1-in-100 bad case, at about 1.00x) and lend the lower amount. Under a normal curve with a 10% standard deviation, P90 is about 87% of P50 and P99 about 77%.
sources: Renewables Valuation Institute, "P50 vs. P99 in Project Finance: How Lenders Size Debt"; Forvis Mazars DSCR page; edbodmer.com wind P99 page (not opened)
use: How to state two numbers at two confidence levels without contradiction: a floor defensible in the 1-in-100 case, a top defensible in the expected case, and an announced gift equal to the lower of what the two tests allow.
critique: The normal curve ignores fat tails (C R02 59). Wind years are independent and stock years are not, so a 1-in-100 year is not a 1-in-100 path. The multiples are convention. Lenders can walk away; Laura cannot.

idea: The cost-overrun facility and the order of call. A committed pre-completion standby is "callable only after contingency is fully used and contractor obligations are enforced", and the sponsor funds "all or a capped portion" last. Worked example (illustrative): budget 1,000, contingency 70 (7%), facility 100 (10%).
sources: Private Equity Bro, "Cost overrun facilities in project finance"; Gowling, Mondaq and rets.ai pieces not opened
use: The FINAL's kept half ("for building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar or a co-sponsor falling short") is a capped standby, called last, after the contractor, insurance, contingency and co-sponsors. Laura's gift is a capped contribution, not a completion undertaking. Say so, because overruns arrive when costs rise (repo check: Taiwan construction cost index +6.53% y/y, Aug 2026).
critique: The contingency size is illustrative, and real overruns are larger (C R05 19). Lenders rarely accept a cap on a completion guarantee. The "cost-to-complete undertaking" label is slightly off.

idea: Contingent support goes uncounted, so price it. "Almost without exception, sponsors' financial reports ignore completion guarantees." Proposed charge = (50% minus P(abandonment)) x mean overrun + P(abandonment) x debt; e.g. a $500m project with $300m debt, a $50m overrun and 1% abandonment gives $27.5m.
sources: IJGlobal, "Quantifying contingent support in project financings"
use: Laura's 2031 range is itself a contingent commitment, and pricing it even roughly is the knowledgeable move for the FR.
critique: One author's proposal, not a standard; the 1% is invented for illustration.

idea: Florence's Monte delle doti (1425). A father deposited money when his daughter was about five, and the fund paid a named sum at marriage after 5-15 years. Depositors were lending to the Commune, which reportedly raided the fund in the 1480s.
sources: Wikipedia "Monte delle doti"; a Unibo article quoting Molho (1994) p.31; Market Histories (a popular site, UNVERIFIED against Molho); Molho, Marriage Alliance in Late Medieval Florence (1994), and Kirshner-Molho (1978), titles only
use: "Same promise, different holder": the instrument has barely changed in 600 years, so what matters is who holds the money. A human story hook for an FR page on why to prefund and why Treasuries.
critique: The payment date was marriage, not fixed, so ages were fudged. The issuer was also the borrower. The return was a lure (11-15%), not a match. A dowry fund had no ladder or matching, so "the same idea" stretches. It had a forfeit feature Laura lacks.
verified: PARTLY; rate CONFLICTING (11-12% against "up to 15%": quote no rate); the 1480s raid UNVERIFIED

idea: Muni escrows and yield burning. Dealers overcharged for the escrow Treasuries in advance refundings. Lehman's 1994 portfolio of $15.8m carried a 0.42% markup, and Lehman agreed to pay $450,151.62 to issuers and $4,520,857.29 to the US Treasury.
use: "Cover after costs": headroom is only real after execution cost. Illustration: 0.42% of a $298k ladder is about $1,250, about two-thirds of the 16 Oct headroom (MODEL, old design). An FR Articulation footnote on real-world execution.
critique: The cases were about tax-arbitrage rules and dealer conduct, not escrow design. WInS charges a flat $10 per bond trade, with no markup.

idea: The debt service reserve account (DSRA), a cash reserve (usually 6-12 months of debt service) for revenue disruption: seems relevant, isn't, because Laura's ladder has no revenue to disrupt. The nearest real thing is the gap between a bond's maturity and its January payment.
use: One sentence: the buffer has a name and a convention. The trap: a DSRA is often a letter of credit (someone else's promise), while Laura's vault is a bond.
critique: S2 called the buffer "about two months" (the old November-maturity design). In the locked TNA, the Feb 2037 bond covers the Jan 2038 payment, a 10.5-month gap with its own reinvestment risk.

idea: The DSCR distribution lock-up. Three zones (target, lock-up, default) give warning room before a cliff, e.g. "nothing goes to the facility while funded cover is below the lock-up level".
sources: Forvis Mazars DSCR page (1.30x lock-up and 1.10x default in the worked example)
use: Could make the 2031 gift decision automatic; S2 says fold it into the Courtroom's lock rather than add a rule.
critique: Large overlap with L-10 and the lock. The page warns that the 1.30x sizing target is not a covenant level.
clash: Partly. A cover-triggered rule adds a trigger beyond the FINAL's two reasons; acceptable only if it limits the gift, never the payments.

idea: Debt sculpting: seems relevant, isn't, because Laura's payments are flat and fixed. But "the ladder is a sculpt in reverse": asset maturities shaped to a liability someone else already shaped.
use: An FR phrase only.

idea: Other project-finance devices, not verified and dropped: equity cure, take-or-pay, hell-or-high-water, PFI availability payments, forward-starting swaps.

idea: The gift range chart and the quiet phase. The lead gift is about 10-20% of the goal; gifts halve in size and double in number down the tiers; the top gifts are raised privately before the public launch; "leadership gifts make up 60% or more".
sources: Funraise gift range chart calculator; Maine State Library campaign FAQ; Nonprofit Quarterly, "The public phase of your capital campaign, part IV"; Soapbox Engage, "Capital campaigns 101: the quiet phase"

critique: Charts come from donor capacity ratings, not a donor's balance sheet. The percentages are consultants' rules of thumb and differ (40-50% against at least 75% raised before launch). A chart can be revised in the quiet phase, and Laura's announced range cannot. Fundraisers say a range invites co-sponsors to plan on the bottom.

idea: The quiet phase is 2028-2030, and the January 2031 move ends it: Laura goes public only when the bottom is owned and the top locked.
sources: S3 §1 fusion hook (the quiet-phase sources above plus the Courtroom lock)

idea: The pyramid multiplier: a short lead gift shrinks every tier below it, so a miss costs the campaign a multiple of Laura's miss. The chain's arithmetic: $25k short on a $150k lead at 10-20% leaves a $125k-$250k hole, 5-10x.
sources: S3 #1's chain; FUSIONS §2 item 8; test T6

critique: Window 28 Oct: unsupported. Neither source says later donors cut their gifts when the lead shrinks, and the chain gives 5-10x, not 3x. Keep "about three times worse" as a stated judgement only.

idea: Campaign-size sanity check: a range Laura can announce of $145k-$170k can credibly lead a campaign of roughly $0.7m-$1.7m (145/0.20 to 170/0.10).
sources: S3's arithmetic on the Funraise and Maine lead-gift shares; the range comes from the 17 Oct range model

critique: It assumes Laura is the lead gift, which the case never says. The range numbers are MODEL (old design).
verified: UNVERIFIED (illustration; "Jun would need to model it")
clash: No, but do not present $145k as a fixed bottom.

idea: Rosenwald's seed, match and sunset. Julius Rosenwald refused a perpetual endowment ("Real endowments are not money, but ideas"), required local communities to match his gifts and funded more than 5,000 one-room schools (4,978 in one exhibit). His fund was spent out in 1948, about a decade before its deadline.
sources: Wikipedia "Rosenwald Fund"; Philanthropy Roundtable, "Debates on perpetuity" and "Julius Rosenwald's timeless legacy of donor intent"
use: FR facility section: Laura's gift is a dated, capped seed that others match, not an operating endowment, and the cap does the sunsetting.
critique: Philanthropy Roundtable is a donor-intent advocacy group. Matching may favour communities that can already pay (not checked). A residency needs running money after the gift, which Rosenwald's model does not answer.

idea: Tobin's rule against spending down. Trustees are "the guardians of the future against the claims of the present" (preserve real value, keep equity among generations), while spend-down donors give it all within a window. Seems relevant, mostly isn't: Laura's plan spends down by design.
sources: Tobin, "What is Permanent Endowment Income?", American Economic Review 64(2), 1974, quoted in Yale's Principles of Investment Management (lecture pdf)
use: FR "considered and rejected", plus the real-versus-nominal point (row 48).
critique: It assumes an endless life and a real target. Neither side has a clean empirical test.
verified: VERIFIED (quote read in the Yale document, not Tobin's paper)

idea: Atlantic Philanthropies' spend-down: the plan was put forward in 2002, spending began in 2012, the foundation closed on 14 Sep 2020, and it gave over $8bn from 1982 to 2020. Rung 1's "closed 2016" was wrong.

idea: Survivorship: "stocks beat bonds over most decades" is the history of the markets that survived (mostly the US). Laura's payments and floor rest on Treasury promises and use no historical sample. Only the top of her 2031 band depends on history.
sources: AMS Feature Column, "The Legend of Abraham Wald" (2016, ams.org/samplings/feature-column/fc-2016-06); Wikipedia "Survivorship bias" (Elton, Gruber and Blake: fund bias 0.9%/yr); Goetzmann and Jorion, "A Century of Global Stock Markets", NBER w5901, and NBER Digest Jul 1997 (US real 4.73%/yr; others' median about 1.5%; world index Survived 5.35%, Continuous 4.86%, Reconstructed 4.74%; markets that became extinct fell 27% the year before their break); Brown, Goetzmann and Ross, "Survival", J. Finance 1995
niche: KNOWN (Wald story is TEXTBOOK; using it to show which number depends on history is NICHE)
use: "The planes we can study are the ones where stocks worked. Laura gets one plane." The floor needs no history; only the top does, and we say so.
critique: The haircut is small for a world index (0.6 pt/yr) and large for a single country. "The US was lucky" can't be proved in advance. VT is a world fund, and JPM's forecasts look forward rather than back. The armour story is mostly legend; Wald actually modelled the missing planes. Scout toy model (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), VT about $31k in Jan 2028): "3 in 4" for the top falls to about 73% with a 0.6 pt haircut and about 68% with 2 pt; P(stocks beat a 5% bond over 10 yrs) is about 62%, or about 47% stressed.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (AMS page, NBER w5901 and Digest, Brown-Goetzmann-Ross record). RG1's "armour where the holes are not" is CONFLICTING (legend, per AMS).
clash: no (the FINAL states no probability; any "3 in 4" must be re-run on the FINAL design)

idea: Ergodicity and gambler's ruin: an average across many investors hides the fact that one investor taking a fixed $50k a year out of shares can run dry, and no later good year brings back a missed payment. So payment safety has to be built in (structural), not left to the odds (statistical).
sources: Peters, "The ergodicity problem in economics", Nature Physics 15 (2019) (coin toss: +50%/-40%; positive average, negative typical path); Doctor, Wakker and Wang, Nature Physics 2020 rebuttal (Tinbergen summary); Wikipedia "Gambler's ruin" (Pascal to Fermat, 1656); Milevsky and Robinson, "A Sustainable Spending Rate without Simulation", FAJ 2005
niche: NICHE (ergodicity framing); gambler's ruin is TEXTBOOK
use: "Laura's wealth grows by multiplication but her payments leave in fixed dollars; the only safe way out is to fix it in dollars with instruments that pay in dollars." Coin toss: the average investor gains, the typical one loses.
critique: Peters is contested ("elementary misunderstandings") and partly restates Kelly/log utility (R02 #34); cite him only with the rebuttal. Ruin here is finite (ten payments) and binary (a broken promise). Scout toy model (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), all-stock, JPM 6.7%/16.47%): about 13% of paths miss a payment (24% under 2 pt stress) while mean terminal wealth is about $0.76m and the median about $0.50m.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (Nature abstract and commented copy; Wikipedia; Milevsky abstract only). RG1's "1654" is CONFLICTING (1656).
where: S4 §2 (l.73-118); RG1 [12] gambler's ruin, ergodicity (l.124, l.126)

idea: Allais and the certainty effect: people give up a lot of expected value for a sure thing. Laura's ten payments are her stated "sure thing" (the case requires it; it's not a taste). The plan is the Allais pattern made consistent: one certain pot and one gamble pot. The twist: certainty costs Laura almost nothing, because the Treasury curve prices the ladder fairly and the unpromised money still buys shares.
sources: Tversky and Kahneman, "Prospect Theory", Econometrica 1979; Wikipedia "Allais paradox" (Allais, Paris conference 1952; Econometrica 1953); R06 D4 (repo: "certainty costs Laura about nothing")
niche: KNOWN (Allais is TEXTBOOK in decision theory; the "hers is cheap" twist is NICHE)
use: "The usual price of certainty is large; hers is small." For the FR's answer to the sceptic.
critique: The paradox describes behaviour, it doesn't justify it ("a bias, not an argument"). Its probabilities are cleaner than any portfolio's. Judges know the certainty effect as a flaw; the reply is that a missed payment is a broken promise, a cliff that dollars don't capture. Savage's own answers UNVERIFIED.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (K&T abstract page; Wikipedia). The R06 D4 cost-of-certainty figure is MODEL (old design) and must be re-run on the FINAL plan.

idea: Contingent immunisation run backwards: CI manages a portfolio actively and locks in a floor only when the cushion runs out. Laura locks first (ladder, then floor) and takes risk only with the surplus. It's CI with the trigger at 100%, the static case, and it gives the plan a lineage practitioners recognise.
sources: Leibowitz and Weinberger, "Contingent Immunization Part I: Risk Control Procedures", FAJ 1982, and "Part II: Problem Areas", FAJ 1983 (rpc.cfainstitute.org); Nasdaq glossary; SuperMoney; CPPI and its 1987 failure (R02 #36)
use: A judge who knows LDI places the plan at once: "CI whose cushion was bought in advance and whose switch is on the calendar, not the market". CPPI failed in 1987 because prices gapped past its trigger; a floor bought in advance can't fail that way.
critique: CI's trigger needs constant monitoring and has gap risk; its active part is bonds, not shares; a manager who can't beat the safety-net yield is just paying for a complicated bond fund. R11: a judge may call the 2031 move "CI with a calendar". Answer: the calendar fits because the liability is created on a date.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (FAJ 1982 abstract; 1983 title only). The 1981 date in RG1 is UNVERIFIED. R11 LISTED.

sources: S4's own reading of Leibowitz-Weinberger; repo headroom "$2k-$5k"

critique: none recorded beyond the CI critique (the deposit itself depends on her income: see rows 30, 33)

idea: Date trigger, not price trigger ("immunise each promise on its birthday"). A promise is matched once it exists: the ten payments exist from the start, so they are bought in 2027; the contribution becomes a promise when Laura names it in 2031, so its top moves into Treasuries before then. That makes the 2031 move a fact about the promise, not market timing or CPPI.
sources: R11 S1 (CI, pension hibernation, Kydland-Prescott R02 #47); S4 §4 (date trigger vs level trigger)
use: A builder buys timber when the contract is signed, not when timber looks cheap and not before anyone has asked for a house. One principle explains all three dates: 2027, 2028 and 2031.
critique: The floor is bought in 2028, three years before its "birthday", so the rule is "on or before", not "on". Rivals also lock in 2031 (9 of 12 scanned), so only the principle is new. A date trigger can't react within the four years.
clash: no (the FINAL moves the other half "before you meet co-sponsors in 2031")

idea: Bullet vs barbell (Fong-Vasicek): bonds that all mature at the payment date (a bullet) deliver in every case. A barbell (short plus long) with the same duration gains a little when all yields move together and loses more when the curve twists. That is why a ladder beat the September IEF/TLT duration match. Test risk payment by payment, not by the whole book's "10-year duration".
sources: Fong and Vasicek, "The Tradeoff between Return and Risk in Immunized Portfolios", FAJ 1983; Fabozzi textbook tradition (RG1); R02 #10, R05 #7
niche: TEXTBOOK (the dollar twist test is a NICHE touch)
use: Every payment has its own bullet, so no curve shape can leave it short. The floor fund is a bullet maturing late 2032. It also answers a judge who sees "10-year duration" and calls the book unhedged.
critique: Low novelty; overlaps R02 #10 and R05 #7. Scout zero-coupon toy (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design), late-Sep 2026 curve 2y 4.81/5y 4.98/10y 5.17): the barbell gains about 0.4-0.5% on a 1 pt parallel move and loses 1.4-3.1% on a twist; on a "$150k floor" a 2% twist is about $3k.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (Fong-Vasicek abstract; the bullet/barbell mapping is the scout's own)
clash: minor: the "$150k floor" is only an illustration; the FINAL and TNA note 2 say the floor fund's payout is not fixed

sources: AnalystPrep CFA III notes on rolldown; repo genius-lab note

critique: Rolldown assumes a static curve and is a mark-to-market idea. T-bills are banned, so the steep short end couldn't be harvested anyway. RG1 said rolldown would grow the 2028 floor; S4 says it doesn't.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (AnalystPrep). RG1's claims are CONFLICTING.

idea: Minimax regret as a cross-check on the 2031 top: pick the figure whose worst "we should have said X" is smallest. With over-promising weighted 3x, it lands within about $1-2k of the newsvendor answer (row 11), so the top isn't an artefact of one method. A 3x3 regret table that co-sponsors can read in ten seconds.
sources: Wikipedia "Minimax regret" (Savage 1951); MetricGate minimax-regret rule page

critique: Sensitive to which states are listed; adding an irrelevant option can flip the answer; ignores likelihood. It shares the 3x input with the newsvendor, so call it "does not contradict", not "proves". Toy model (ILLUSTRATIVE, MODEL (old design)): about $16.4-17.2k above the floor vs the newsvendor's about $15.5k.

idea: Dutch book as a consistency audit: never state a probability you wouldn't bet at. "Certain" must mean exactly what the instruments back (nominal Treasury dollars on the date held) and nothing wider. Any figure that appears in both the IPS/TNA and the FR must describe the same event with the same number. "Upside for free above a guaranteed floor" is the one inconsistent promise.
sources: Wikipedia "Dutch book" (Ramsey 1926; de Finetti 1931); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Dutch Book Arguments"
use: A check table, run across the IPS, TNA and FR, of every probability or figure stated, with its event and source.
critique: It tests coherence, not truth. It assumes you'd bet at your stated odds, and co-sponsors aren't bookmakers. Judges may find it remote. A range plus a probability is automatically coherent. It's a discipline, not a selling point.
verified: VERIFIED by S4 (Wikipedia, SEP). The no-arbitrage bridge is the scout's own and has no citation.
clash: no. Use it as a check: TNA note 1 says "near-ironclad guarantee" and TNA note 3 cites "about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan)", so the FR must match both (see row 69)

idea: S4's argument chain: histories show only survivors (row 1); averages hide ruin (row 2); so safety must be built in, not left to the odds; that means a ladder matched payment by payment whose guarantee uses no history. Allais (row 3) shows why that feels right, R06 D4 shows it's nearly free, and minimax (row 10) checks the one number that does depend on history.
use: A four-step "answer to the sceptic" section in the FR.
critique: Every step's numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE and need re-running.

idea: Two-sided refutation: name the strongest objection a professional would raise and answer it in the same text. That beats a one-sided case; naming an objection and leaving it unanswered is worse than silence.
sources: Wikipedia "Inoculation theory" (McGuire 1961); O'Keefe meta-analysis (107 studies, 20,111 people), reported at spring.org.uk; Allen 1991 (26 studies), reported at customerthink.com
use: Pick one real objection ("a Treasury ladder gives up ten years of growth", "the floor isn't fixed" or "the top isn't a promise") and answer it with the plan's own fact.
critique: "Inoculation" is the wrong mechanism: it's resistance to a later attack and fades (about 13 days). The useful finding is the sidedness meta-analysis. A straw-man objection backfires with an expert judge. There's no "judges already agree, so skip it" exception.
verified: VERIFIED by S5 through secondary reports only; McGuire's 1961 original UNVERIFIED

idea: Pratfall: one small, priced admission from a plainly competent author raises trust. Five admissions, or a weak opening, don't.
use: Name the one real soft spot (reinvestment of coupons and the maturity gap; the floor fund's payout isn't fixed), its cost, and what absorbs it. Like a pilot who says which instrument is out and why it doesn't matter on this route.
critique: It's a liking result about a taped quiz contestant, not credibility in writing. It needs competence shown first. High-self-esteem observers prefer the flawless version. A planned admission isn't an accident. Modest evidence: a tiebreak, not a pillar. Uses the about $21k coupon gap, MODEL (old design).
clash: no (TNA note 1 already names the reinvestment risk; TNA note 2 names the NAV payout)

idea: Stackelberg commitment: moving the promised half of VT into Treasuries before 2031 turns an announcement (cheap talk) into a leader's commitment that co-sponsors can build on. It recasts the 2031 move as credibility, not just safety.
sources: Stackelberg 1934 (RG1); Schelling on commitment (background, not opened); cheap talk (R02 #45)
use: A ferry captain who says "I won't leave until the boat is full" gets a full boat only if the engines are visibly switched off. The move into Treasuries is the engine switched off.
critique: "Stackelberg" is often name-dropped for any first mover; it needs the move to be visible and irreversible, and Laura could legally sell.
clash: no (matches the FINAL: "whatever figure you choose is money you already own")

idea: Varian's crowding-out warning: in a public-good game, a leader's large gift can lower total giving. Frame the 2031 range by the gap it leaves for others, and offer a match, rather than headlining Laura's maximum. Includes RG1's challenge grants (a gift paid only once matching money is raised).
sources: Varian, "Sequential contributions to public goods", J. Public Economics 1994 (via CESifo WP 2602, ifo.de); Karlan and List on matching gifts (R05 #18); challenge grants (RG1)

critique: The model assumes a smooth public good with no fixed cost and no warm glow. Field and lab evidence is mixed. Co-sponsors give for relationship and status. Any number depends on a facility cost the case doesn't give.
verified: VERIFIED by S5 (CESifo paper quoting Varian's abstract); challenge grants UNVERIFIED (RG1 low)

idea: Assurance contract with a refund: the bottom is owned and unconditional; everything above it is given only if the facility really goes ahead, and otherwise it stays Laura's. Co-sponsors' pledges, likewise, are paid only if the building is real.
sources: Bagnoli and Lipman, Review of Economic Studies 56(4), 1989 (ideas.repec.org); conditional promises (R05 #17); Andreoni seed money (R02 #46); dominant assurance contracts UNVERIFIED
use: Kickstarter's all-or-nothing rule: "you are only charged if it funds". The cap protects Laura's flexibility; the refund protects co-sponsors' trust.
critique: The model needs a known cost and complete information, and the case gives no facility cost. A badly set threshold fails. Only the refund rule is new.
clash: no (fits the half "promised to no one")

idea: Focal points vs precise numbers: publish the bottom precisely (it's owned and computed) and the top as a round, goal-like number, rounded down and never up.
sources: Wikipedia "Focal point (game theory)" (Schelling 1960; 36 of 40 chose $50); Mason, Lee, Wiley and Ames 2013 (ScienceDaily: a precise offer gives "the illusion they have done their homework"); Pope and Simonsohn 2011 (ScienceDaily: .300 vs .299 batting average)
use: How to write the numbers of the 2031 range in the fundraising text.
critique: The precise-offer study is hypothetical haggling, and the batting averages are self-set goals (SAT 1390 vs 1400 made no difference). Focal points need a shared culture, which co-sponsors in Taiwan and the US may not have. The two effects pull in opposite directions. Modest.
verified: VERIFIED by S5 (Wikipedia; two ScienceDaily pages)
clash: caution: the file mentions a "$145k bottom (the $150k floor rounded down)" (old design). The FINAL and TNA give no figure and say the floor payout isn't fixed. Rounding a computed bottom down is consistent; a fixed $150k is not.

idea: Bayesian persuasion used as an honesty test: a signal can't raise the receiver's average belief. So the range should leave co-sponsors expecting, on average, the same gift as Laura's own central estimate. That makes "credible" testable.
sources: Kamenica and Gentzkow, "Bayesian Persuasion", AER 2011 (Stanford PDF; prosecutor example: prior 0.3, 60% convicted)
use: The prosecutor example as a cautionary tale: this is what a range built to persuade would look like, and ours deliberately isn't.
critique: As a tool it is ethically backwards (it pools good and bad states so the receiver acts when she shouldn't). It needs commitment to the signal and Bayesian receivers. Matching gifts break the model. The plan doesn't change.
verified: VERIFIED by S5 (paper PDF); the Bayes-plausibility line is UNVERIFIED (a standard result)

idea: Narrow bracketing: judging each choice separately can produce a combination that is worse in every state of the world. "Ten brackets for the payments, one bracket for the portfolio." A rival who holds shares while paying to insure them in the same account holds that dominated pair. Judges should read the whole plan, not trade by trade.
sources: Read, Loewenstein and Rabin 1999 (not opened); Rabin and Weizsäcker, AER 99(4), 2009 (RePEc: 28% chose dominated combinations)
use: One paragraph in the FR's Investment Concepts; also a reminder to name the bracket (all three deliverables are judged together).
critique: The experiments use lotteries, not dated payments. Narrow bracketing is right when liabilities really are separate. Partly decoration.
verified: VERIFIED by S5 (2009 paper via RePEc); 1999 original UNVERIFIED

idea: Swiss cheese and common-cause failure: count failures by cause, not by component. Laura's layers (the reinvested coupons, the 2028 deposit, the share cushion) may share one hole: a recession that lowers yields, cuts her writing income and drops shares all at once. R11 L4 adds that held-to-maturity bonds don't mind falling prices; their only weakness is yields falling for good, which usually comes with the same slump. A 2022-style year (yields up, shares down) opens a different pair of holes.
sources: Reason, "Human error: models and management", BMJ 2000;320:768-770 (PMC1117770); US NRC common-cause failure document ML082350989; Wikipedia, Fukushima (10 of 13 cooling systems lost; the one air-cooled generator survived); 10 CFR Part 50 App. A (single-failure rule; Criterion 22 on diversity) (Cornell LII); Reason 1990 (RG1)
use: Fukushima had many backups in one basement: "three locks keyed alike are one lock". This extends the FINAL's career point: her income, her shares and her coupon reinvestment can all suffer in the same slump. That is why each payment rests on a bond already bought, not on future income or shares.
critique: It's a metaphor, not a calculation. Redundancy arithmetic assumes independent failures. It earns its place only by naming a specific shared cause. Bond yields falling in recessions is "standard, not sourced". There is no joint probability (Jun to model).
verified: VERIFIED by S6 (BMJ, NRC, Wikipedia, CFR); recession co-movement UNVERIFIED
clash: no; strongly supports CAREER. R11 L4's "2033 re-match placed where the two risks meet" isn't in the FINAL (see row 82).

idea: Certainty over the whole chain, not per payment: ten payments in series fail if any one fails. "99% safe per year" is about 90% over ten years (0.99^10), the same way a "100-year flood" has about a 9.6% chance in ten years. State "a high degree of certainty" for all ten payments together.
sources: USGS, "Floods and recurrence intervals" (LISTED); reliability mathematics
use: "Certainty for all ten, not each one."
critique: Floods are nearly independent from year to year; Laura's risks share one cause. The lesson is the unit, not the formula.

idea: "Correlation makes the chain certain" (R11 L1): if each payment were a separate 99% bet, Laura would miss one in about one decade in ten. Because every rung is a debt of one issuer, the ten risks collapse into one, the risk every "risk-free" benchmark already assumes away. For the payments, the plan deliberately doesn't diversify.
sources: R11's own logic; US default and debt-ceiling risk (R02 #13)
use: "For the payments, we deliberately did not diversify." That cuts against the textbook.
